entities.summary:
Marcus of Viterbo (1304–1369) was an Italian Franciscan who played a pivotal role in shaping the Catholic Church during the Middle Ages. He rose through the ranks of the Franciscan order, becoming Minister General in 1359 and subsequently appointed as a papal legate in 1366. This marked a significant shift in the Church's relations with European monarchs and the rise of the papacy as a dominant force in medieval politics.

Marcus's appointment as Cardinal in 1366 further solidified his influence within the Church, cementing his position as a key figure in the Church's hierarchy. His papal legatary role allowed him to mediate disputes between the Church and European states, demonstrating the increasing importance of the papacy in international relations.

Despite his significant influence, Marcus's legacy has been somewhat overshadowed by that of his contemporaries, such as Pope John XXII. However, his contributions to the Church's governance and diplomacy during this period remain an important chapter in the history of the Catholic Church.

The lasting impact of Marcus of Viterbo can be seen in the Church's continued emphasis on its diplomatic role in European politics, as well as its ongoing efforts to maintain its authority in the face of encroaching secular power.
